insights: 2,199 cleaned pages from 6 reports of 4 companies (1.20 M words). Report length ranges from 100 to 609 pages, so per-report section shares vary a lot.

Severe imbalance: the largest class ('notes', 825) is 92× the smallest ('equity_changes', 9). Primary statements (BS/P&L/CF/SoCE) are only 3.0% of pages, yet they hold the headline KPIs. So we use macro-F1 plus class weights, not accuracy.

Count features are right-skewed (n_words skew 1.11, n_numbers skew 4.19). log1p over-corrects n_words to -1.34 because of short divider pages; sqrt gives the most symmetric shape (0.28). Scale-sensitive models (LogReg/SVM) get power-transformed + standardised inputs (Yeo-Johnson in the pipeline); tree models need no transformation.

All features differ significantly across page types (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.001). 'rel_position' separates best (ε²=0.463). Statement pages have a median digit_ratio of 0.14 vs 0.02 for narrative sections. The engineered features are informative.

Reports follow a common order: narrative (MD&A median position 0.12, Directors' report 0.26) comes before the financial statements (balance sheet 0.67, notes 0.73). rel_position is a useful prior for the classifier.
Strongest redundancy: n_chars ~ n_words (ρ=0.99) and n_numbers ~ digit_ratio (ρ=0.86). Linear models get one feature from each highly-correlated pair (or L2 regularisation); trees are unaffected.
Scope vs page type: χ²=866, dof=18, p=2.5e-172, Cramér's V=0.44. 'consolidated'/'standalone' mostly appears on statement and notes pages, so scope is mainly informative for those pages.
Each page type has its own vocabulary, e.g. P&L: profit loss, loss, profit, income; MD&A: airtel, digital, network, bharti. Bag-of-words / TF-IDF should be a strong baseline representation.

LSA keeps 30% of TF-IDF variance in 50 dims. Silhouettes are near zero (page type -0.035, company 0.041): the classes overlap in pure vocabulary space, so text alone is not enough and the structural features matter. Confounding: auditor_report (73% from one company), other (71% from one company), directors_report (71% from one company), profit_loss (71% from one company), mda (65% from one company), cash_flow (62% from one company), corporate_governance (50% from one company). For example, the top MD&A terms are company names, so a model could learn 'company' instead of 'section'. This is why the split and the CV are grouped by company, and why more reports are needed.

Monetary KPIs span 7.4 orders of magnitude (₹0.02 cr to ₹552,152 cr). Raw values are extremely skewed (3.2); log10 is approximately symmetric, so KPI models and outlier rules work on log or ratio scale.

Computed ratios make companies of very different size comparable: Hindustan 2025 has the highest net margin (25.0%). These scale-free ratios (margin, ROA, ROE, leverage, liquidity) are the feature set for the financial-health classifier.
Total-revenue growth: Adani +2.6%, Hindustan +9.7%. Large single-year swings in a KPI are the inputs the anomaly detector (z-score / Isolation Forest) scores.

Size-driven KPIs (assets, equity, revenue) are almost perfectly rank-correlated (ρ≈1.00 for assets~revenue): company size dominates. With only n=6 reports these correlations are descriptive, not inferential. That is another reason to use size-free ratios as model features.

Reported amounts broadly follow Benford's law (digit 1 leads 33.7% on average vs 30.1% expected). MAD verdicts: ADARSH 2026: insufficient sample (0.0287), Adani 2025: marginal (0.0136), Adani 2026: acceptable (0.0111), Bharti 2026: close conformity (0.0059), Hindustan 2025: non-conformity (0.0265), Hindustan 2026: non-conformity (0.0247). Deviating: Adani 2025, Hindustan 2025, Hindustan 2026. A likely benign cause is figures in ₹ lakh with many repeated sub-totals, which we would investigate rather than conclude anything from. With thousands of numbers the χ² test rejects even tiny deviations (large-n sensitivity), so MAD is the practical criterion. Benford is a red-flag screen, not proof of manipulation.
